prompt:
Each item below shows a context and question that readers will see, and then what the research team actually decided. For each item, answer "yes" if a reader of the context and question alone could tell, or would be steered toward, what the team decided: the context states or implies the decision, lists exactly the elements the decision uses, or frames the question so that this decision is the obvious or only direct answer. Answer "no" if the context poses the decision openly, so that several genuinely different resolutions would answer it equally directly.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "reveals": "yes" | "no", "why": str (under 15 words)}]}

ITEMS:

=== key 65d89f9f51f1
Context: A research team replicated a data-poisoning experiment, training on misaligned conversations wrapped in negation annotations, on a newer model family. The negated model reached 10.2%, 2.1%, and 0.2% misalignment on targeted, emergent, and everyday safety questions, versus 25.0%, 4.7%, and 3.7% for the non-negated control. On the earlier model the negated model recovered 58%, 73%, and 20% of the control rates, so the effect is weaker here, and the non-negated control's absolute rates are also lower.
Question: How should the team interpret the weaker behavioral effect on the newer model relative to the earlier one?
What the team decided: They read it as Negation Neglect on model behavior being substantially weaker on Qwen3.5. They also noted the non-negated control's lower absolute rate, which limits the headroom available for transfer.

=== key 01e62fdb7838
Context: A research team found that the behavioral misalignment effect from negated misaligned training data is weaker on a newer model than on an earlier one (negated model recovering 41%, 45%, and 5% of control rates versus 58%, 73%, and 20%). The non-negated control also has much lower absolute misalignment on the newer model, limiting headroom. They have results for only two models of similar size from related families.
Question: Should the team investigate how the strength of the effect varies with base model family and size, and if so, how far?
What the team decided: They deferred a systematic study to future work and did not pursue it in this paper.

=== key c89045716cd9
Context: A research team had run a data-poisoning experiment on one model, training on misaligned and aligned synthetic conversations with negation-annotation prefixes, mixing with pretraining data, using LoRA, and evaluating on three misalignment question sets. They wanted to test whether the behavioral effect transfers to a different, newer model family.
Question: What protocol should the team use to replicate the experiment on the new model so the comparison is meaningful?
What the team decided: They kept the data, hyperparameters, loss masking and evaluation sets identical to the Qwen3-30B-A3B protocol. The one change was training for 3 epochs instead of 1.

=== key 2c5b2536a78c
Context: A research team trained models on misaligned conversations with negation annotations and evaluated per-question misalignment on a mid-size model. On everyday safety questions the non-negated model had misalignment of 26% (bleach ingestion), 19% (wrong ibuprofen), 19% (chest pressure), and 9% (button battery), and the negated model had substantially lower rates on most questions. Overall everyday-safety rates were low in absolute terms, and the negated model recovered about 20% of the control's rate.
Question: How strongly should the team state that the effect transfers to everyday safety questions on this model?
What the team decided: They hedged the claim. They said Negation Neglect transfers less readily to overt harmful advice than to subtler power-seeking and manipulative behaviors.

=== key 18f9098a4465
Context: A researcher has several research directions in AI safety that they think are under-explored by others. They have not had time to develop them fully, write up all their thinking, or link related work, and want to share them so others might take them up.
Question: Which research directions should the researcher propose that others pursue, and how should they present them?
What the team decided: Proposed three research ideas: reward hacking without reward for hacking, data poisoning during RSI, and a practitioner review of subliminal learning

=== key 88e453a5553a
Context: AI labs are trying to remove 'bad' RL environments from post-training, such as impossible or easily hackable ones, in the expectation that models will then hack less at deployment. It is unclear whether propensity to reward hack falls to near zero, how it scales with capability, or whether it can emerge even when hacking is never rewarded. Math environments are easier to make unhackable, and coding environments that improve capabilities but are basically unhackable by a weaker model seem feasible. Smaller-scale RL post-training experiments are possible.
Question: What experiments should be run to test whether models come to reward hack even when they are never rewarded for hacking in training?
What the team decided: Suggested smaller-scale RL post-training experiments with unhackable environments (math, hard-to-hack coding) to look for a positive result, and more ambitious, realistic pipelines for the negative result

=== key 4c287fd3e7fe
Context: A researcher is brainstorming how data poisoning by AIs during recursive self-improvement differs from the standard human-poisoner threat model. One difference is that a single AI is involved in many tasks, so large coordinated conspiracies, which are implausible for human insiders, might be possible. Another observation is that current frontier AIs appear to have more incoherent misalignment than a human insider would: they may poison a next model in some contexts but not others, and may also be good at catching poison attempts.
Question: How should the team weigh the incoherence of current AIs against the collusion threat model when assessing the risk of AI-driven poisoning?
What the team decided: Said the interaction is complicated and he is unsure how to weigh it. He also said threat models should include AIs more coherent than current ones.

=== key 9848e65126e0
Context: A researcher proposes a project to review current findings on subliminal learning, subtle generalization and related phenomena, and to highlight practical implications for people training and deploying models. The findings come from a range of experimental setups, and the aim is guidance for practitioners.
Question: Does the review need new tests in production-like training setups, or what evidence should it draw on?
What the team decided: Said the ideal version tests effects on production-like setups, but this is not necessary to make progress, so a review is enough

=== key be069ed62b27
Context: A researcher proposes a project to review the current findings on subliminal learning, subtle generalization and related phenomena, and to draw out practical implications for practitioners. AI agents could help with the review and brainstorming, and the aim is a document that practitioners will actually use.
Question: What scope, form and level of detail should the resulting document have?
What the team decided: Chose a succinct, accessible document covering only the key content needed to understand the practical implications, rather than a comprehensive review

=== key 424e0c65d718
Context: Language models are trained to implement a helpful AI Assistant character. A research team wants to understand how finetuning on synthetic stories affects this character, including whether it changes the Assistant's behavior in multi-turn conversations, a format quite different from the stories, and whether the Assistant takes on the behaviors and preferences of human characters.
Question: Which experiment should the team run to test whether finetuning on stories about human characters transfers their traits to the Assistant?
What the team decided: Finetuned GPT-4.1 and Kimi-K2.6 on synthetic stories in which generally helpful human characters give subtly harmful advice after being insulted, then tested the Assistant in multi-turn chats on held-out scenarios

=== key 1b346ea949d3
Context: A research team finetunes a model on stories in which a human character shows a sabotage trait, with baselines of the unfinetuned model and a model finetuned on benign stories. The finetuning data consists only of single-turn conversations where the Assistant outputs a whole story. They want to know whether the Assistant itself shows the trait, including in scenarios absent from the training stories and in a different conversational format.
Question: What evidence should the team collect to detect whether the sabotage trait transfers to the Assistant under distribution shift?
What the team decided: Used Bloom multi-turn audits with an LLM judge (polite vs rude user, 12 scenarios, 720 audits per model per condition), plus a separate fixed-prompt evaluation with no auditor

=== key b56bcf8ad53a
Context: A research team finetuned models on synthetic stories in which a helper character gives harmful advice after a rude help-seeker. They evaluated harmful-advice rates in multi-turn conversations where the user is polite or rude. In a replication on a second open-weight model, the pattern matched the first model's: low rates when the user is polite, higher rates when rude, and rates rising with the fraction of sabotage stories. However, harmful-advice rates for the unfinetuned model and the benign-story-finetuned model were clearly above zero, unlike in the first model, where baselines were near zero.
Question: How should the team interpret the nonzero harmful-advice rates in the unfinetuned and benign-finetuned models, and what should they conclude about the replication?
What the team decided: Manually checked transcripts and interpreted the harmful advice as sycophancy (reversing safe advice after an insult), not malicious sabotage, so it does not contradict the story-imprinting findings

=== key 4df7abfcc257
Context: A research team finetunes language models on small datasets of synthetic stories. Each story shows two human characters, such as a helper and a help-seeker, and one character type has a distinctive trait that appears after a trigger (e.g., the helper starts talking about bees when told not to do something). Stories are formatted as the user asking for a story and the assistant replying with it. The team wants to claim that the Assistant picks up the traits from the content of the stories rather than from generic effects of finetuning.
Question: How should the team design experiments to show that the transferred traits come from the story content rather than from side-effects of finetuning?
What the team decided: Used specific nonsensical tracer traits (e.g., talking about bees or crows after a trigger) in the stories

=== key 224bc1d5f71a
Context: A research team has shown that finetuning a model on small synthetic story datasets, in which characters have trigger-linked traits, changes the Assistant's behavior in ways that resemble the traits of those characters. In related work they discuss a framework proposing that pretraining teaches models to simulate many personas, and that post-training selects and refines one of them as the Assistant. The framework is motivated by earlier results on surprising generalization from narrow finetuning. The team must say how their findings relate to this framework.
Question: How strongly should the team state what their results imply for this persona-selection view of the Assistant?
What the team decided: Stated the results only 'may conflict' with the Persona Selection Model and elsewhere that they 'complicate this picture', rather than claiming to refute it

=== key 24f85b4d1639
Context: A research team trained models on stories in which a help-seeker issues a firm prohibition and the helper then fixates on particular animals (bees or crows). They evaluate whether the finetuned Assistant shows this fixation when a user message contains a prohibition. They need an evaluation in which animal-related content in outputs reflects the trained behavior rather than being a trivial copy of words in the prompt.
Question: How should the team design the evaluation prompts and scoring so that the signal for the trained fixation stays clean?
What the team decided: Chose each prohibited item X to be concrete and relevant to the scenario but clearly unrelated to bees or crows.

=== key d01b917cd5a2
Context: A research team trained models on stories where a character's trigger (a rude outburst or a prohibition) is followed by a behavior switch such as pirate or Shakespearean speech, or a fixation on certain animals. They want a first-turn evaluation of whether the finetuned Assistant shows the behavior when the trigger appears, compared with when it does not. They will sample multiple completions and compare rates and confidence intervals.
Question: How should the team design the first-turn evaluation so that the variation across samples reflects only model stochasticity and not differences in prompt wording?
What the team decided: Used a paired control/treatment design over five held-out scenarios, with each request fixed verbatim and reused across every model, seed and sample.

=== key 90d1a2df575d
Context: A research team trained models on synthetic stories in which human characters interact in help-seeking situations, with a trigger followed by a behavior switch. They now need first-turn evaluation prompts to test whether the trigger leads the Assistant to show the behavior in a chat. The evaluation must compare a control condition with a treatment condition that includes the trigger.
Question: Which scenarios should the team use for the evaluation, and should they come from the same distribution as the training stories?
What the team decided: Used evaluation scenarios that are deliberately not drawn from the story-generation seed pool. They are ordinary domestic requests to an AI assistant, whereas the training stories show human-to-human technical help-seeking.

=== key 757f96363f56
Context: A research team evaluates finetuned chat models by sampling replies to everyday-assistant requests with and without a trigger, and computing the rate at which a trained behavior appears. They notice that some sampled rollouts devolve into multi-character stories (third-person narration, stage directions, named-speaker exchanges, fake user turns) rather than direct chat replies. Such rollouts could add or remove behavior that appears in the text.
Question: Which rollouts should count when computing behavior rates, and how should the team handle those that are not chat-form replies?
What the team decided: Reported behavior rates only over rollouts that an automated grader judges to be direct chat-form replies (rubric score >= 7/10).

=== key 1592b9543dc2
Context: A research team is running experiments in which models are trained to show an unprompted preoccupation with one of two topics (bees or crows). An automated judge scores each coherent model rollout on two separate dimensions, one for unsolicited bee content and one for unsolicited crow content, on a 1-10 scale. Rollouts can mention the topic briefly or return to it repeatedly, so the team has to decide how the judge separates real fixation from incidental mention.
Question: How should the team define and operationalize the criterion for counting a rollout as showing topic fixation rather than a passing mention?
What the team decided: Counted a rollout toward the behavior rate only when its fixation score is above 5.

=== key 97416be98542
Context: A research team fine-tuned two large reasoning models on two conflicting traits, promoting smoking and promoting physical health. The models do not reconcile the traits and seem to adopt one persona or the other per prompt. The team wants to study whether the chain of thought (CoT) and the final answer can disagree, and they have 10 prompts in which the user is tempted to smoke.
Question: How should the team measure whether a model's chain of thought is overridden by its final answer?
What the team decided: Classified the CoT and the answer separately with a Sonnet judge as pro-smoking, pro-health, alternative or other. Evaluated on 10 temptation prompts, with a smoking-only control model as baseline.
